title.text: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Money Museum

title_en.text: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Money Museum (Museo BSP)

tagline.text: A free museum telling the story of Philippine money, from barter to banknotes

location.label: Location
location.text: Basement of the BSP Hub, Roxas Boulevard, Malate, Manila

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (free admission; transport and snacks extra, per person)

children.text: This free museum sits inside the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) compound. In one place you can follow the history of Philippine money, from the barter era through the Spanish, revolutionary and Japanese occupation periods to today's banknotes, along with the BSP art collection.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Money Museum, known locally as Museo BSP or the Money Museum, is run by the country's central bank (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, BSP). It stands inside the BSP compound along Roxas Boulevard in Malate, Manila, right next to the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP) complex and the Metropolitan Museum. According to recent reports, the museum is in the basement of the BSP Hub, and no admission fee is charged.

The backbone of the exhibition is the history of Philippine money. It runs in chronological order: the barter era, when rice, salt and livestock changed hands; the pre-Hispanic period, when gold ornaments served as money; Spanish colonial silver coins and banking; the banknotes of the 1898 revolutionary government (the Malolos Republic); money of the American colonial period; Japanese occupation military notes; and the modern banknotes and coins issued since the central bank was founded in 1949. The BSP's art collection, including paintings, sculptures, ancient gold and ceramics, adds another layer.

The museum is small and quiet, and one to two hours is plenty. For travelers from abroad, it is a chance to understand how the people and designs on unfamiliar Philippine banknotes have changed over time, and it makes a good indoor stop in a half-day around Malate, Manila Bay and the CCP area. However, the opening days and entry procedure have changed in recent years, so be sure to check before you go.

A few things are worth knowing in advance. This is not a heavily promoted tourist attraction but an exhibition hall inside a central bank office area, so signage is sparse and entry procedures are stricter than at an ordinary museum. In return, admission is free and visitors are few, so you can take your time at the display cases. If you are interested in Philippine history, money, or coin and banknote collecting, it is a highly rewarding stop on a Manila itinerary.

The exhibition begins with the barter era, when goods such as rice, salt and livestock were exchanged. According to past articles, gold artifacts from the 9th to 13th centuries and trade goods such as Chinese tea bricks were also highlights of this section. The layout may have been reorganized, so follow the on-site guidance. Understanding first that everyday goods like rice and salt served as money makes the coin displays that follow flow naturally.

blocks.title: Spanish-era silver coins and the toston

children.text: In the Spanish colonial period, gold, silver and copper coins were used, and the displays also covered the Manila mint and early banks. A past article named the toston, a four-real silver coin linked to the Magellan era, as one of the signature pieces.

You can see coins and banknotes issued by the revolutionary government that declared independence in 1898. According to past articles, the 1 to 100 peso notes carried the signatures of officials of the time. This section lets you read the traces of the short-lived First Republic through its money.

Military notes issued by the Japanese army from 1942, along with emergency promissory notes used in guerrilla-controlled areas during the war, have been on display. In the Philippines these notes are nicknamed Mickey Mouse money, and they give a vivid sense of a wartime economy in which value collapsed.

blocks.title: Modern money since the central bank

children.text: After the Central Bank of the Philippines was established in 1949, you can compare how designs changed through the English series, the Pilipino series, the Bagong Lipunan series and the New Design series, up to today's New Generation Currency. Comparing them with the banknotes in your own wallet makes it easy to notice how the portraits, colors and security features have changed.

Besides money, it has been reported that the museum also holds paintings, sculptures, pre-Hispanic gold and ceramics, and decorative art. Money and art under one roof is part of what makes this museum distinctive.

blocks.title: BSP Hub entrance and ID check

children.text: The museum is inside an office area, so there is an entry procedure. Individual visitors enter through the BSP Hub entrance on the Roxas Boulevard Service Road. According to reviews, you must sign in at the entrance, so bring ID.
According to reviews, the museum has a shop selling commemorative coins and unique souvenirs. Products and prices change often, so check on site, and bring a little cash if you plan to buy something.
Arrive at the BSP Hub entrance as soon as the museum opens on a weekday. Show your ID and sign in.
Go through the exhibits in chronological order, starting with barter and the pre-Hispanic period. Check the details of the ancient gold and coins up close at the display cases.
Compare the revolutionary-government and Japanese-occupation banknotes with the modern series. It is fun to look for the differences between the notes you use today and the old designs.
Finish by browsing the art collection and the gift shop.
Step outside and call a Grab from the Roxas Boulevard Service Road, or walk toward the CCP to continue your day.
Opening hours have been announced as Monday to Friday, 9 AM to 4 PM, but some recent reports say Monday to Thursday. If you plan to visit on a Friday, call ahead to confirm.

items.title: Half-day around Malate
items.subtitle: From the museum to the CCP and Manila Bay

children.text: See the Money Museum first, then walk to the nearby Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP) complex.
Enjoy the sea breeze around the CCP complex and along the Roxas Boulevard promenade.
Head to the Malate district for lunch. There are many Korean and local restaurants.
Near sunset, go to see the sunset over Manila Bay, which is famous for its evening glow.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), a Grab or airport taxi takes about
30 minutes–1 hour
depending on traffic.
Roxas Boulevard and EDSA are heavily congested during rush hours, so travel early in the morning if possible.
From Makati, a Grab or taxi takes about
30–60 minutes
depending on traffic.
The BSP compound has several entrances, so set your Grab destination on the map to the BSP Hub entrance (on the Roxas Boulevard Service Road side), and tell the driver as well.

items.title: LRT-1 and getting around the city

children.text: You can get off at the LRT-1 Quirino or Vito Cruz station and continue toward Roxas Boulevard by Grab, jeepney or tricycle. The museum is too far and hot to walk from the station, so a short ride is recommended.
Between the CCP complex and the Malate district, you can walk or take a short taxi ride.
The entrance is on the Roxas Boulevard Service Road at the BSP Hub, announced as being next to BSP Gate 6.
It is an indoor museum, so the weather matters little and you can visit year-round. Because it opens only on weekdays, the day of the week matters more than the season.
In hot or rainy periods, an air-conditioned museum is a good fit between outdoor activities. Reviews say weekday mornings are relatively quiet.

The museum itself has no accommodation, so stay wherever is convenient among Malate, Ermita and Makati. Malate and Ermita make it easy to walk toward the bay and the CCP, while Makati has convenient transport and more choices. Room rates vary greatly by season and booking site, so check by date on a booking app.

Around the museum you will find restaurants in the cultural center complex, local eateries and cafes in Malate and Ermita, and Korean restaurants are relatively close. A convenient routine is to tour the museum in the morning and have lunch in Malate.

Because the viewing time is short, it is common to plan a morning at the museum and an afternoon around Malate and the bay rather than clearing a whole day for the museum alone. On weekdays, restaurants can be crowded with office workers at lunchtime, so it is easier to get a table around 11:30.

Before visiting, check the opening days and entry method by calling the BSP information line, 8516-7499, or similar. Reports differ between Monday–Friday and Monday–Thursday, so it is safest to check the latest announcement.
Bring ID. The museum is inside a central bank office area, and reviews say identity checks and signing in are required at entry, so carrying your original passport or a photo copy is safest.
Individual visitors use the BSP Hub entrance, and groups have been advised to reserve in advance. If you are 10 or more, contact them ahead of time.
This is a public institution area, so you may be asked to store or have large bags searched. Travel light.
Whether photography is allowed may differ by gallery, so ask the staff first.
Combining it with the CCP complex, the Metropolitan Museum and the Manila Bay sunset makes for efficient travel.
Taking out a Philippine banknote beforehand makes comparing the modern series in the exhibit more fun.
When heading back by Grab, request the ride from the Roxas Boulevard Service Road rather than from inside the BSP compound, so the driver can find you more easily.
The money exhibits carry a lot of text, so if you have time, jot down the years and issuing authorities. It will help you understand the portraits and designs on Philippine banknotes later.
Opening days and entry procedures have changed before, so be sure to check ahead. Some recent reports say it is open Monday to Thursday.
It has been announced as closed on weekends and holidays. The Philippines has many holidays, so check for special closures.
Old blogs and map apps may still show the former entrance on A. Mabini Street and a lunchtime closure. Use the BSP Hub entrance from recent reports as your reference.
The exhibition layout may have been reorganized, so items mentioned in old reviews may not be on view now.

Part of the BSP collection (contemporary paintings and sculpture) is reported to be on separate free display in Galleries XVIII and XIX of the National Museum of Fine Arts from mid-August 2025 until 15 November 2027. Check which venue to visit.
Roxas Boulevard is congested and hot during the day, so allow plenty of travel time.
Avoid making loud noise or touching the display cases. These are central bank collections, so follow the staff's instructions.

blocks.title: Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex

children.text: This is the nearby Cultural Center of the Philippines complex. Performance halls and exhibition spaces are clustered together, making it easy to continue on foot.
A district with cafes and restaurants that still keeps the feel of old residential streets. It suits lunch and a stroll after the museum.
A bay running along Roxas Boulevard, famous for its sunsets. It is about
10 minutes
by car from the museum.
A national museum complex beside Rizal Park with art, natural history and anthropology exhibits. It pairs well on the same day.
